APMO 2009 Problem 3

GeometryTrianglesArea
Game: Move a triangle whose base and height stay the same, and see which shape makes the three heights multiply to the biggest number; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag A, B or C along its line, or drag the small handle on the height line. Focus a point and use the arrow keys; tick the boxes for the two hints.

Drag a point, or focus it and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

The triangle can slide its top corner A sideways without changing its base BC or its altitude h. Yet the product of all three altitudes changes a lot. The surprising part is that the shape the original page names as the best is only the best for some base lengths.

Turn heights into one side product

Let A', B', C' be the feet of the three altitudes. The base and height of the triangle never change, so its area S is fixed. Twice that area can be written with any side as the base:

2S = AA' · BC = BB' · AC = CC' · AB

Multiply the last two forms. Because (BB' · AC)(CC' · AB) = (2S)² stays the same, making the altitude product AA' · BB' · CC' as big as possible is exactly the same as making the side product AB · AC as small as possible. The line through A is fixed, so only the sideways position of A matters.

Where AB × AC is really smallest

Put the middle of BC at 0, let half the base be a, the height be h, and let u be how far A is to one side of the middle. Then

AB² · AC² = (u² + a² + h²)² − 4a²u²

This is smallest at u = 0 when h ≥ a, that is when the base BC is at most twice the height. Only then is the isosceles triangle with AB = AC the answer, as the page says. When the base is longer than twice the height, the smallest value is at u² = a² − h²: that is where the angle at A is a right angle (A lies on the circle with diameter BC), and AB · AC = BC · h. The logic test checked this over a grid of bases, heights and positions: in that long-base range the isosceles point actually gives the smallest product of altitudes among its neighbours. The page's claim is therefore false there, and the status line says so as you drag.

What S above T does and does not prove

The page uses the circumcircle: 4R · S = AB · BC · AC, so with BC and S fixed, a smaller side product means a smaller circumradius R. Let T be the position of A with TB = TC and S the topmost point of the circle through A, B, C. S really is always at or above T; with M the middle of BC this says SM ≥ TM (the page writes A'), with equality exactly at AB = AC. The test confirmed that for every position in the grid. But the page then reads off that R is smallest at T, and that step fails when the base exceeds twice the height: there the circle of a right triangle has its centre at A' itself and radius a, smaller than the radius at T.

Tick both hints, then drag B outward until the base is longer than twice the height. Slide A along its line and watch the percentage in the status line: it peaks at a right angle at A, not when S touches T.
